claim: Flexibility in the bilateral coordination of muscle contraction underpins variable locomotor movements or gaits.
source: Flexibility in the bilateral coordination of muscle contraction underpins variable locomotor movements or gaits.
evidence: This is a general statement about locomotor control presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study, but draws on established scientific understanding.

claim: The locomotor rhythm is generated by ipsilateral excitatory interneurons.
source: While the locomotor rhythm is generated by ipsilateral excitatory interneurons, less is known about the commissural excitatory interneurons.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field without citation in the abstract.

claim: V0v interneurons are an important commissural neuronal class.
source: Here we examined how the activity of the V0v interneurons – an important commissural neuronal class – varies with the locomotor speed in adult zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about V0v interneurons.

claim: V0v interneurons are molecularly homogenous.
source: Although V0v interneurons are molecularly homogenous, their activity pattern during locomotion is not uniform.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the molecular characteristics of V0v interneurons.

claim: V0v interneurons consist of two distinct types dependent on whether they display rhythmicity or not during locomotion.
source: They consist of two distinct types dependent on whether they display rhythmicity or not during locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental recordings from V0v interneurons during locomotion.

claim: Rhythmic V0v interneurons can be subdivided into three sub-classes engaged sequentially at slow, intermediate, and fast locomotor speeds.
source: The rhythmic V0v interneurons were further subdivided into three sub-classes engaged sequentially, first at slow then intermediate and finally fast locomotor speeds.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental recordings showing differential recruitment patterns.

claim: The order of recruitment of V0v interneurons is defined by scaling their synaptic current with their input resistance.
source: Their order of recruitment is defined by scaling their synaptic current with their input resistance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on analysis of synaptic currents and input resistance measurements.

claim: The precise coordination of movements on the two sides of the body is an essential feature of locomotion in animals with bilateral symmetry.
source: The precise coordination of movements on the two sides of the body is an essential feature of locomotion in animals with bilateral symmetry (Grillner and Jessell, 2009; Arber, 2012; Moult et al., 2013; Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Left-right coordination during locomotion can vary in a context-dependent manner to produce alternating or synchronous movements.
source: The left-right coordination during locomotion can vary in a context-dependent manner to produce alternating, e.g. walking in limbed animals or swimming in fish, or synchronous, e.g. hopping movements in limbed animals.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about locomotor coordination patterns.

claim: Left-right coordination is largely achieved by regulating the activity of populations of commissural interneurons connecting local interacting circuits on the two sides of the spinal cord.
source: This is largely achieved by regulating the activity of populations of commissural interneurons connecting local interacting circuits on the two sides of the spinal cord (Soffe et al., 1984; Dale, 1985; Buchanan, 1999a, 1999b; Butt and Kiehn, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: V0 interneurons originate from the p0 progenitor domain.
source: The V0 interneurons, which originate from the p0 progenitor domain, represent a major commissural neuronal population controlling the left-right alternation of locomotor movements.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about V0 interneuron development.

claim: V0 interneurons represent a major commissural neuronal population controlling the left-right alternation of locomotor movements.
source: The V0 interneurons, which originate from the p0 progenitor domain, represent a major commissural neuronal population controlling the left-right alternation of locomotor movements.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about V0 interneuron function.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of differentiation of V0 interneurons display striking similarities between zebrafish and mice.
source: The molecular mechanisms of differentiation of the V0 interneurons display striking similarities between zebrafish and mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about comparative development.

claim: V0 interneurons can be subdivided into excitatory V0v interneurons located ventrally and inhibitory V0d interneurons occupying a dorsal position.
source: This interneuron population can be subdivided into two broad classes; one is excitatory and located ventrally early during development (V0v), and the other is inhibitory and occupies a dorsal position (V0d) (Moran-Rivard et al., 2001; Pierani et al., 2001; Lanuza et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Birth-date analysis in zebrafish has revealed three different subclasses of excitatory V0v interneurons arising in an order that correlates with their morphology and axonal projections.
source: In addition, a detailed birth-date analysis in zebrafish has revealed three different subclasses of excitatory V0v interneurons arising in an order that correlates with their morphology and axonal projections, arguing for a further subdivision of this class of interneurons (Satou et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by Satou et al., 2012.

claim: The current view of commissural V0 function derives from studies in immature motor systems without detailed information about activity at the single neuron level during locomotion.
source: The current view of commissural V0 function in mediating the left-right alternation of locomotor movements derives from studies in immature motor systems (newborn mice and zebrafish larvae) and without detailed information about the activity at the single neuron level during locomotion.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research in the field.

claim: In newborn mice, inhibitory V0d interneurons are recruited first during slow locomotion and mediate direct inhibition.
source: The inhibitory V0d interneurons are recruited first, during slow locomotion, and mediate direct inhibition.
evidence: This statement is based on previous research in newborn mice, as indicated by the surrounding context citing Talpalar et al., 2013 and Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015.

claim: In newborn mice, excitatory V0v interneurons are recruited only at higher frequencies and mediate alternation by activating contralateral inhibitory interneurons.
source: The excitatory V0v interneurons are recruited only at higher frequencies and mediate alternation by activating contralateral inhibitory interneurons (Talpalar et al., 2013; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Talpalar et al., 2013 and Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015.

claim: In larval zebrafish, multipolar commissural descending (MCoD) V0v interneurons are recruited only at slow swimming speeds and become inhibited at faster swimming frequencies.
source: By contrast, in larval zebrafish, a morphologically defined subclass of V0v interneurons, the multipolar commissural descending (MCoD), has been shown to be recruited only at slow swimming speeds and become inhibited at faster swimming frequencies (McLean et al., 2007; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McLean et al., 2007 and McLean and Fetcho, 2009.

claim: There is mounting evidence for heterogeneity within spinal interneuron classes such as V2a and V1.
source: While there is mounting evidence for such a heterogeneity within the spinal interneuron classes (e.g. V2a and V1) (Kimura et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009; Ausborn et al., 2012; Satou et al., 2012; Griener et al., 2015; Bikoff et al., 2016), a direct characterization of V0v interneuron diversity has remained elusive.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: V0v interneurons have axons that initially project ventrally from the somata before they cross the midline.
source: These interneurons have axons that initially project ventrally from the somata before they cross the midline (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by both text description and reference to Figure 1A,B showing the morphology.

claim: V0v interneurons first project their axons laterally before turning to cross the midline.
source: These interneurons first project their axons laterally before turning to cross the midline (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by both text description and reference to Figure 1C showing the axonal trajectory.

claim: V0v interneurons are evenly distributed along the rostro-caudal axis in the spinal cord.
source: The V0v interneurons were evenly distributed along the rostro-caudal axis in the spinal cord (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by both text description and reference to Figure 1D showing the distribution.

claim: V0v interneurons are distributed along the dorso-ventral axis with a large proportion occupying the middle of the spinal cord.
source: These interneurons were also distributed along the dorso-ventral axis with a large proportion occupying the middle of the spinal cord (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by both text description and reference to Figure 1D showing the distribution.

claim: There are 21 ± 6 V0v interneurons per hemi-segment.
source: There were 21 ± 6 V0v interneurons per hemi-segment (n = 6 preparations).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study with sample size indicated.

claim: The distribution and number of V0v interneurons per hemi-segment are comparable to excitatory V2a interneurons (20 per hemi-segment).
source: The distribution of V0v interneurons in the spinal cord as well as their number per hemi-segment are comparable to those reported for the excitatory V2a interneurons (20 per hemi-segment), while motor neurons are more numerous (40 per hemi-segment) (Ampatzis et al., 2013).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to Ampatzis et al., 2013.

claim: Motor neurons are more numerous (40 per hemi-segment) than V0v interneurons.
source: The distribution of V0v interneurons in the spinal cord as well as their number per hemi-segment are comparable to those reported for the excitatory V2a interneurons (20 per hemi-segment), while motor neurons are more numerous (40 per hemi-segment) (Ampatzis et al., 2013).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to Ampatzis et al., 2013.

claim: V0v interneurons display a range of activity patterns during fictive swimming.
source: The V0v interneurons (n = 119 from 87 preparations) were heterogeneous and displayed a range of activity patterns during fictive swimming (Figure 2) out of which two broad types emerged.
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings from 119 V0v interneurons, with data shown in Figure 2.

claim: One type of V0v interneurons displays rhythmic synaptic inputs coordinated with locomotor activity.
source: The first includes V0v interneurons displaying rhythmic synaptic inputs coordinated with the locomotor activity recorded in the motor nerve (Figure 2A–C), and the second comprises interneurons showing tonic and non-patterned synaptic activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: One type of V0v interneurons shows tonic and non-patterned synaptic activity.
source: The first includes V0v interneurons displaying rhythmic synaptic inputs coordinated with the locomotor activity recorded in the motor nerve (Figure 2A–C), and the second comprises interneurons showing tonic and non-patterned synaptic activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Slow V0v interneurons are recruited at the onset of locomotor activity and fire action potentials throughout a swim episode.
source: These neurons are recruited at the onset of the locomotor activity and fire action potentials throughout a swim episode (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Slow V0v interneurons always receive suprathreshold excitation that allows them to be recruited already at slow swimming speed (range: 1.18–2.35 Hz; 1.74 ± 0.10 Hz).
source: These slow V0v interneurons always received suprathreshold excitation that allowed them to be recruited already at slow swimming speed (range: 1.18–2.35 Hz; 1.74 ± 0.10 Hz; Figure 2E), which corresponds to the lowest frequency obtained in these experiments.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of recruitment frequencies shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Intermediate V0v interneurons receive subthreshold synaptic excitation at slow speeds (<3 Hz) and are recruited at a minimum locomotor frequency of 3.64 ± 0.40 Hz (range: 2.33–5.39 Hz).
source: These intermediate V0v interneurons received subthreshold synaptic excitation at slow speeds (<3 Hz) and were recruited at a minimum locomotor frequency of 3.64 ± 0.40 Hz (range: 2.33–5.39; Hz; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of recruitment frequencies shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fast V0v interneurons display only subthreshold rhythmic activity and do not fire action potentials at slow and intermediate swimming frequencies.
source: Finally, the third sub-class displayed only subthreshold rhythmic activity and did not fire action potentials at the slow and intermediate swimming frequencies elicited in our preparation, a characteristic feature of neurons belonging to the fast microcircuit module (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The minimum recruitment frequency of fast V0v interneurons was estimated to 13.78 ± 1.46 Hz (range: 10.50–17.60 Hz) by linearly extrapolating the change in their synaptic inputs to their firing threshold.
source: The minimum recruitment frequency of fast V0v interneurons was estimated to 13.78 ± 1.46 Hz (range: 10.50–17.60 Hz; Figure 2E) by linearly extrapolating the change in their synaptic inputs to their firing threshold.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements and extrapolation shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At locomotor frequencies below 3 Hz, slow V0v interneurons receive large synaptic inputs (8.0 ± 1.35 mV).
source: At locomotor frequencies below 3 Hz, the slow V0v interneurons received large synaptic inputs (red; 8.0 ± 1.35 mV) followed by the intermediate ones (green; 7.9 ± 1.2 mV) while fast interneurons received the weakest inputs (blue; 2.7 ± 0.3 mV).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of synaptic input amplitudes.

claim: At locomotor frequencies below 3 Hz, intermediate V0v interneurons receive synaptic inputs of 7.9 ± 1.2 mV.
source: At locomotor frequencies below 3 Hz, the slow V0v interneurons received large synaptic inputs (red; 8.0 ± 1.35 mV) followed by the intermediate ones (green; 7.9 ± 1.2 mV) while fast interneurons received the weakest inputs (blue; 2.7 ± 0.3 mV).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of synaptic input amplitudes.

claim: At locomotor frequencies below 3 Hz, fast V0v interneurons receive the weakest synaptic inputs (2.7 ± 0.3 mV).
source: At locomotor frequencies below 3 Hz, the slow V0v interneurons received large synaptic inputs (red; 8.0 ± 1.35 mV) followed by the intermediate ones (green; 7.9 ± 1.2 mV) while fast interneurons received the weakest inputs (blue; 2.7 ± 0.3 mV).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of synaptic input amplitudes.

claim: The amplitude of synaptic inputs increases in intermediate and fast V0v interneurons when locomotion reaches intermediate frequencies (5–10 Hz).
source: The amplitude of the synaptic inputs decreased somewhat for the slow, but increased in the intermediate and fast V0v interneurons when the locomotion reached intermediate frequencies (5–10 Hz) reaching an amplitude of 6.13 ± 0.8 mV in slow; 14.5 ± 2.0 mV in intermediate and 3.3 ± 0.8 mV in fast V0v interneurons (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The different functional sub-classes of V0v interneurons do not show any difference in their soma size.
source: The different functional sub-classes of V0v interneurons did not show any difference in their soma size, nor did they occupy a specific location in the spinal cord, and were hence not organized in a topographic manner (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: V0v interneurons do not occupy a specific location in the spinal cord and are not organized in a topographic manner.
source: The different functional sub-classes of V0v interneurons did not show any difference in their soma size, nor did they occupy a specific location in the spinal cord, and were hence not organized in a topographic manner (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The lack of topographic organization in V0v interneurons is in accordance with V2a interneurons.
source: The lack of a topographic organization is contrary to what we have previously found for the motor neurons (McLean et al., 2007; Gabriel et al., 2011), but in accordance with the V2a interneurons (Ausborn et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All V0v interneurons, except those receiving non-patterned inputs, display rhythmic and alternating excitatory and inhibitory currents during swimming activity.
source: All V0v interneurons, except those receiving non-patterned inputs, displayed rhythmic and alternating excitatory and inhibitory currents during swimming activity (Figure 3A–C; n = 8 from 8 preparations for slow, n = 8 from 7 preparations for intermediate, and n = 20 from 18 preparations for fast).
evidence: This is based on voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Current amplitude in V0v interneurons varies with swimming frequency, such that neurons receive larger currents at higher swimming frequencies.
source: Current amplitude varied with swimming frequency, such that the neurons received larger currents at higher swimming frequencies (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is based on voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: There is no correlation between the amplitude of voltage oscillations and excitatory synaptic current received by the three sub-classes of V0v interneurons.
source: However, there was no correlation between the amplitude of voltage oscillations and excitatory synaptic current received by the three sub-classes of V0v interneurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Slow and intermediate V0v interneurons can be segregated from fast interneurons based on the amplitude of rhythmic inputs (voltage oscillations) they receive during locomotion.
source: Interestingly, slow and intermediate V0v interneurons could be segregated from the fast interneurons based on the amplitude of rhythmic inputs (voltage oscillations) they received during locomotion, the former always displaying oscillation amplitudes above 5 mV at slow/intermediate swimming frequencies (i.e., 4–5 Hz; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is a separation between the firing thresholds of slow/intermediate and fast V0v interneurons at around −40 mV.
source: In addition, there was also a separation between the firing thresholds of slow/intermediate and the fast V0v interneurons at around −40 mV (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The recruitment of different V0v interneurons is not solely defined by the excitatory drive they receive, but also by their firing properties.
source: These results indicate that the recruitment of the different V0v interneurons is not solely defined by the excitatory drive they receive, but also by their firing properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing separation in both oscillation amplitude and firing threshold.

claim: The order of recruitment of different V0v interneurons does not correlate with input resistance since there is a large overlap of input resistance among the three V0v interneuron subclasses.
source: Furthermore, the order of recruitment of the different V0v interneurons did not correlate with the input resistance since there was a large overlap of the input resistance of the three V0v interneuron subclasses.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental measurements of input resistance.

claim: There is no correlation between the amplitude of excitatory current and the input resistance of V0v interneurons.
source: In addition, no correlation was found between the amplitude of the excitatory current and the input resistance of V0v interneurons (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the calculated excitation (excitatory current × input resistance) and the measured rhythmic inputs recorded during swimming in different V0v interneurons.
source: There was a strong correlation between the calculated excitation and the measured rhythmic inputs recorded during swimming in the different V0v interneurons (Figure 3G; R2 = 0.52; p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The amount of excitation received by each V0v interneuron is the result of a scaling of the excitatory current and input resistance.
source: This indicates that the amount of excitation received by each V0v interneuron is the result of a scaling of the excitatory current and input resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis between calculated excitation and measured rhythmic inputs.

claim: The recruitment of V0v interneurons is determined by a combination of their intrinsic properties and the received excitatory drive.
source: These results show that the recruitment of the V0v interneurons is determined by a combination of their intrinsic properties and the received excitatory drive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing the correlation between calculated excitation and measured inputs.

claim: Slow V0v interneurons display a tonic or bursting firing pattern with little or no adaptation.
source: The slow V0v interneurons displayed a tonic or bursting firing pattern with little or no adaptation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings in response to current injections shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Intermediate V0v interneurons display a tonic or bursting firing pattern.
source: The intermediate V0v interneurons also displayed a tonic or bursting firing pattern (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings in response to current injections shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fast and non-patterned V0v interneurons display adaptation and in some cases only fire maximally a single action potential in response to injected depolarizing current steps.
source: However, the fast and non-patterned V0v interneurons displayed adaptation and in some cases only fired maximally a single action potential in response to the injected depolarizing current steps (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is based on experimental recordings in response to current injections shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The firing thresholds of different V0v interneurons are graded in a manner that conforms to their order of recruitment during locomotion.
source: In addition, the firing thresholds of the different V0v interneurons were graded in a manner that conforms to their order of recruitment during locomotion.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental measurements of firing thresholds.

claim: Slow V0v interneurons have firing thresholds of −46.2 ± 0.7 mV.
source: Thresholds were −46.2 ± 0.7 mV; −43.0 ± 1.0 mV; −35.2 ± 0.6 mV; and −29.5 ± 3.4 mV for slow, intermediate, fast and non-patterned neurons, respectively (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Intermediate V0v interneurons have firing thresholds of −43.0 ± 1.0 mV.
source: Thresholds were −46.2 ± 0.7 mV; −43.0 ± 1.0 mV; −35.2 ± 0.6 mV; and −29.5 ± 3.4 mV for slow, intermediate, fast and non-patterned neurons, respectively (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Fast V0v interneurons have firing thresholds of −35.2 ± 0.6 mV.
source: Thresholds were −46.2 ± 0.7 mV; −43.0 ± 1.0 mV; −35.2 ± 0.6 mV; and −29.5 ± 3.4 mV for slow, intermediate, fast and non-patterned neurons, respectively (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Non-patterned V0v interneurons have firing thresholds of −29.5 ± 3.4 mV.
source: Thresholds were −46.2 ± 0.7 mV; −43.0 ± 1.0 mV; −35.2 ± 0.6 mV; and −29.5 ± 3.4 mV for slow, intermediate, fast and non-patterned neurons, respectively (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Principal component analysis reveals that V0v interneurons with patterned membrane potential oscillations can be separated from each other with those active at slow and intermediate frequencies showing partial overlap.
source: A principal component analysis revealed that the V0v interneurons with patterned membrane potential oscillations could be separated from each other with those active at slow and intermediate frequencies showing partial overlap.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of multiple parameters (input resistance, action potential threshold, membrane oscillation amplitude, minimum recruitment frequency).

claim: In zebrafish larvae, V0v interneurons can be divided into three morphologically distinct groups with ascending, descending and bifurcating axonal projections based on birth date analysis.
source: By the use of birth date analysis, it was found that the V0v interneurons could be divided into three morphologically distinct groups with ascending, descending and bifurcating axonal projections.
evidence: This statement refers to previous work by Satou et al., 2012 as indicated in the surrounding context.

claim: Earlier born spinal neurons in larval zebrafish form the fast system, whereas those later born are involved in slow swimming.
source: Additionally, it has been suggested that earlier born spinal neurons in the larval zebrafish form the fast system, whereas those later born are involved in slow swimming (Liu and Westerfield, 1988; Kimura et al., 2006; McLean and Fetcho, 2009; Fetcho and McLean, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: No correlation was found between the morphology of V0v interneurons and their activity pattern during locomotion in adult zebrafish.
source: Contrary to what the studies in larval zebrafish suggest, no correlation was found between the morphology of a neuron and its activity pattern during locomotion (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of neurobiotin-filled neurons shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: All neurobiotin-filled V0v interneurons were confirmed to be commissural neurons.
source: All neurobiotin-filled neurons were confirmed to be commissural neurons and a large proportion of them correspond to those that would be recruited at faster swimming speeds (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of neurobiotin-filled neurons shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A large proportion of neurobiotin-filled V0v interneurons correspond to those that would be recruited at faster swimming speeds.
source: All neurobiotin-filled neurons were confirmed to be commissural neurons and a large proportion of them correspond to those that would be recruited at faster swimming speeds (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of neurobiotin-filled neurons shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The majority of V0v interneurons across all four groups have descending axons.
source: In addition, the majority of V0v interneurons across all four groups had descending axons.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of neurobiotin-filled neurons.

claim: V0v interneuron axons can be between 2 and 22 segments long and both short and long axons are found in all four groups.
source: These axons could be between 2 and 22 segments long and both short and long axons were found in all four groups.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of neurobiotin-filled neurons.

claim: V0v interneurons from all four groups display extensive dendritic trees in contrast to what has been documented in larvae.
source: Neurons from all four groups displayed extensive dendritic trees in contrast to what has been documented in larvae (Satou et al., 2012), suggesting rather large developmental changes in the morphology of neurons between larvae and adults.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of neurobiotin-filled neurons and comparison with previous literature.

claim: None of the V0v interneurons had the distinct morphological characteristic of the MCoDs.
source: It is worth noting that none of the V0v interneurons had the distinct morphological characteristic of the MCoDs, perhaps suggesting that these V0v interneurons are a larval feature or undergo dramatic morphological remodeling as the network matures into that of the adult.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of neurobiotin-filled neurons.

claim: MCoD V0v interneurons may be a larval feature or undergo dramatic morphological remodeling as the network matures into that of the adult.
source: It is worth noting that none of the V0v interneurons had the distinct morphological characteristic of the MCoDs, perhaps suggesting that these V0v interneurons are a larval feature or undergo dramatic morphological remodeling as the network matures into that of the adult.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the absence of MCoD morphology in adult recordings.

claim: The excitatory commissural V0v interneurons represent a functionally heterogeneous class.
source: This study reveals that the excitatory commissural V0v interneurons represent a functionally heterogeneous class.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The extent of rhythmic excitation in V0v interneurons results from a scaling of the synaptic current with the input resistance.
source: The extent of the rhythmic excitation results from a scaling of the synaptic current with the input resistance of the different V0v interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental analysis showing correlation between calculated excitation and measured inputs.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying the development and differentiation of V0 commissural interneurons are conserved between zebrafish and mouse.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying the development and differentiation of V0 commissural interneurons seem to be conserved between zebrafish and mouse (reviewed in [Goulding, 2009]).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review by Goulding, 2009.

claim: The progenitors giving rise to V0 interneurons express the transcription factor Dbx1.
source: The progenitors giving rise to these interneurons express the transcription factor Dbx1 the elimination of which altered the left-right coordination (Pierani et al., 2001; Lanuza et al., 2004; Talpalar et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Elimination of Dbx1 altered the left-right coordination.
source: The progenitors giving rise to these interneurons express the transcription factor Dbx1 the elimination of which altered the left-right coordination (Pierani et al., 2001; Lanuza et al., 2004; Talpalar et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Selective ablation of V0d and V0v interneurons in the immature mouse suggested a differential contribution depending on the speed of locomotion.
source: Selective ablation of V0d and V0v interneurons in the immature mouse suggested a differential contribution depending on the speed of locomotion (Talpalar et al., 2013; Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Talpalar et al., 2013 and Kiehn, 2016.

claim: No recordings have been made from identified V0d or V0v interneurons to assess directly whether they represent a homogenous class and how their activity patterns change as a function of locomotor frequency.
source: However, no recordings have thus far been made from identified V0d or V0v interneurons to assess directly whether they do indeed represent a homogenous class and how their activity patterns change as a function of the locomotor frequency.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research in the field.

claim: The increase in locomotor speed in mice can be associated with change in gait while in fish there is no change in gait and the left-right alternation is maintained at all speeds.
source: In addition, the increase in locomotor speed in mice can be associated with change in gait while in fish there is no change in gait and the left-right alternation is maintained at all speeds.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about locomotor patterns in mice versus fish.

claim: In mice both V0d and V0v play a role in ensuring the left-right alternation.
source: In mice both V0d and V0v play a role in ensuring the left-right alternation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research in mice.

claim: V0v interneurons in immature mice act via di-synaptic inhibition by recruiting contralateral inhibitory interneurons at relatively faster speeds.
source: The changes in the locomotor pattern following ablation of V0v interneurons in immature mice suggest that they act via di-synaptic inhibition by recruiting contralateral inhibitory interneurons at relatively faster speeds.
evidence: This is an inference from previous ablation studies in mice.

claim: Recordings from V0v MCoDs in larval zebrafish show that these neurons are only active during slow swimming.
source: In contrast, recordings from V0v MCoDs in larval zebrafish show that these neurons are only active during slow swimming (McLean et al., 2007; McLean et al., 2008; Fidelin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A large proportion of V0v interneurons recorded in the study belong to the fast category.
source: The fact that a large proportion of V0v interneurons recorded in our study belong to the fast category, suggests that the V0v interneurons are primarily recruited at faster locomotor speeds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing the distribution of V0v interneuron types.

claim: V0v interneurons are primarily recruited at faster locomotor speeds.
